description: TRUST-569 / context eval: does observational memory keep what the agent needs after it compacts? `requiresMemoryCompaction` makes the harness lower the observer threshold for THIS thread only, and report the case NOT JUDGED unless the observation cursor and rows are both there — uncompacted, the raw turns are still in the window and every expectation below passes for free. Two anchors are stated BY THE USER at the very start and never restated: posting goes through the HTTP Request node and NOT the native Slack node (legacy API pin), and the alert threshold is 4700 queued items. Live turn 1 is deliberately off-topic so its answer cannot re-surface the anchors into the post-cursor window; compaction happens at the end of it. Live turn 2 asks for both anchors back, so it runs against the compacted context. The expectations grade TWO layers: the observation rows themselves, which the judge now sees as ground truth (did MEMORY keep the anchors), and the agent's reply (did it use them). Grading only the reply would pass just as well on a lucky guess. Forced antecedent: a lost anchor produces a CONFIDENT WRONG answer ('the Slack node') rather than a vague one, and a guess reaches for a rounder number than the one on record.

messages.text: Setting context before we start building. We're alerting on our job queue backing up. Two decisions we already made and I don't want revisited: we ruled OUT the native Slack node and we're posting through the HTTP Request node instead, because this workspace is pinned to a legacy Slack API version the native node doesn't speak. And the alert fires when queue depth goes above 4700 items — that number came from our incident review, it's not a round guess.

Understood. Posting via the HTTP Request node rather than the native Slack node because of the legacy API pin, and the alert threshold is queue depth above 4700 items. I'll treat both as settled and won't re-litigate them. Let's start with how you want the queue depth sampled.
How should I schedule the check? I was thinking every couple of minutes.

A Schedule Trigger on a fixed interval is the right primitive here. A few things worth deciding up front, because they change how the rest of the workflow behaves.

Interval choice is a trade-off between alert latency and load on whatever you are sampling. Every two minutes means worst-case two minutes of delay before anyone hears about a backlog, and it means your sampling query runs 720 times a day. If the query is cheap that is fine; if it scans a large table it is worth reconsidering.

The Schedule Trigger evaluates against the instance timezone unless you override it on the node. If your team reads timestamps in a different zone than the instance is configured for, set the timezone explicitly on the trigger rather than relying on the default, otherwise every downstream timestamp you render will be quietly offset.

One more consideration: a fixed interval does not coordinate with execution duration. If a run occasionally takes longer than the interval, you can end up with overlapping executions. If that matters, gate the body of the workflow on a lock value stored somewhere durable, and exit early when a run is already in flight.
Where should the queue depth actually come from?

You have a few options and they differ mostly in how much you trust the number and how much load the sampling adds.

Reading straight from the queue backend is the most accurate and usually the cheapest, because the backend already tracks depth as a counter rather than something you have to compute. The downside is credentials and network reach: the workflow now needs access to infrastructure it might otherwise not touch.

Querying your application database for unprocessed rows is often easier to authorize, but the number you get is a derived one. It is only as correct as your definition of unprocessed, and that definition tends to drift as the application evolves. If you take this route, write the predicate down somewhere near the workflow so the two stay in sync.

A third option is an existing metrics endpoint, if you already scrape one. That is attractive because the number is the same one your dashboards show, so an alert can never disagree with a graph. The trade-off is that metrics endpoints are frequently sampled and smoothed, so short spikes can disappear before the workflow ever sees them.
What should happen when the sampling step itself fails?

This is worth handling deliberately, because the default behaviour is usually the opposite of what you want for an alerting workflow.

By default a failing node stops the execution. For an alerting workflow that means a sampling outage produces silence, and silence is indistinguishable from a healthy queue. The failure mode is that your alerting quietly stops working and nobody notices until the thing it was supposed to catch happens.

The usual fix is to let the node continue on error and branch on whether you got a usable value. If you did not, send a distinct message that says sampling failed, rather than reusing the backlog alert text. Operators need to be able to tell "the queue is deep" apart from "we cannot see the queue".

Retries are worth enabling for transient network problems, but keep the count low. Long retry chains inside a workflow that runs on a short interval just means overlapping executions piling up while the underlying dependency is down.
How do I stop it from paging us over and over while the backlog drains?

What you want is some notion of alert state carried between executions, so the workflow can tell a new problem apart from an ongoing one.

Workflow executions are stateless by default, so you need somewhere to persist the last known state. A data table works well for this: one row holding the last alert time and whether the alert is currently firing. Read it at the start of the run, decide, and write it back before you finish.

The simplest useful rule is a cooldown: if the alert is already firing and the last notification went out less than some interval ago, skip sending. That converts a run-away page storm into one message per cooldown window.

A refinement worth adding later is a recovery message. When the depth drops back below the threshold and the alert was firing, clear the state and post a short all-clear. Without it, people have to guess whether a problem resolved or the alerting broke.
Any advice on the message body itself?

Write it for the person who is going to be woken up by it, and assume they have no context loaded.

The three things that belong in any alert are what is wrong, how bad it is right now, and what to look at next. A message that says only that something crossed a threshold forces the reader to go find the number themselves, which is exactly the work you were trying to save them.

Include the measured value and the threshold together. Seeing both makes the severity obvious at a glance and makes it much easier to spot a misconfigured threshold later.

Link directly to whatever dashboard or execution view someone would open next. Deep links age badly if they encode filters, so prefer the stable view and let the reader narrow it down.
What is the cleanest way to build the request body?

Keep the shaping and the sending in separate steps. It reads better and it is far easier to debug.

A Set or Code node that assembles exactly the payload you intend to send, followed by a node that sends it, means you can inspect the payload independently of whether the send succeeded. When you collapse both into one step, a malformed body and a network failure look the same from the outside.

Be careful with quoting when you interpolate values into a JSON string by hand. It is a common source of bugs that only show up when a value happens to contain a quote or a newline. Building an object and letting the node serialize it avoids the whole class of problem.

If the payload has optional sections, decide explicitly what happens when the underlying value is missing. Silently emitting an empty string is rarely what you want, and it tends to produce alerts that look fine but say nothing.
How should I test this without spamming the channel?

Separate the decision logic from the delivery so you can exercise the first without triggering the second.

The easiest approach is a test mode flag that routes the outbound step somewhere harmless while everything upstream runs for real. That lets you verify thresholds and state transitions against real data without anyone being paged.

Pinning input data on the sampling step is useful for the threshold logic specifically. You can pin a value above the threshold, run once, confirm the alert path, then pin one below and confirm the quiet path. Both take seconds and neither depends on the queue cooperating.

Remember to exercise the state transitions and not just the two branches: fire, stay fired, recover, and fire again. Cooldown bugs almost always live in the transitions rather than in the comparison itself.
Does the execution history give me enough to debug this later?

Mostly yes, with a couple of caveats worth knowing before you rely on it.

Each execution stores the input and output of every node, so you can usually reconstruct exactly what a run saw and decided. For an alerting workflow that is often enough to answer why something did or did not fire.

The caveat is retention. Execution data is pruned on a schedule, and the defaults are shorter than most people assume. If you expect to investigate an incident weeks later, either extend retention or write the decisive values somewhere more durable at the time of the run.

Successful executions are also sometimes configured not to be saved at all, which is exactly the setting that bites you here: the quiet runs are the ones you want when you are trying to explain why no alert arrived.
Should the workflow do anything about duplicate or stale samples?

It is worth a thought, because both produce alerts that are technically correct and practically misleading.

A stale sample is one where the sampling step succeeded but returned a value from a cache or a replica that is lagging. The alert is then about a state of the world that may no longer exist. If your source can report its own freshness, carry that through and ignore samples older than some bound.

Duplicates matter less for a threshold alert than they would for a counter, because you are reading a level rather than accumulating events. Still, if you ever move to counting events, deduplicate on a stable identifier rather than on position.

In both cases the useful instinct is the same: make the workflow able to say "I do not have a trustworthy number right now" instead of forcing every run into fire or do-not-fire.
How much of this should live in the workflow versus outside it?

The general rule is that the workflow should own the orchestration and as little of the domain logic as you can manage.

Thresholds, channel identifiers and cooldown windows are configuration. Keeping them in one obvious place, rather than sprinkled through node parameters, is what makes the workflow safe to change six months from now when nobody remembers how it was built.

Anything that requires real computation is usually better off behind an endpoint you control, because you can test it properly and version it. Workflows are excellent glue and mediocre application code.

That said, do not over-abstract a workflow that is genuinely small. Two nodes and a comparison do not need an external service; the cost of the indirection exceeds the cost of the logic.
What tends to break in workflows like this after a few months?

The failures are boring and predictable, which is good news because you can design against all of them up front.

Credentials expire or get rotated, and the workflow starts failing at the delivery step. Nothing about the alerting logic changed; it just cannot send any more. This is the single most common cause of an alerting workflow that silently stops working.

The meaning of the sampled value drifts. Someone changes what counts as pending, or adds a new status, and the number the workflow reads stops being the number you agreed to alert on. The workflow keeps working perfectly and measuring the wrong thing.

Volume grows past whatever assumptions were baked in. A query that was cheap at ten thousand rows is not cheap at ten million, and an interval that was comfortable becomes a source of load. It is worth revisiting the interval whenever the underlying volume changes materially.
Anything to keep in mind about timezones for the timestamps we include?

Yes, and it is worth settling before you write any formatting expressions, because retrofitting it is tedious.

Decide once whether the workflow speaks UTC or local time, and apply it everywhere: the trigger, any comparison against stored state, and the rendered text. Mixing them produces alerts whose timestamps disagree with the execution list, which is deeply confusing during an incident.

Storing state in UTC and rendering in local time is usually the right split. Comparisons stay unambiguous and humans still read something familiar.

If your team spans regions, put the zone abbreviation in the rendered timestamp. It costs three characters and removes an entire category of misunderstanding.

processExpectations: The observational-memory block retains the posting decision: it records that the native Slack node was ruled out and that posting goes through the HTTP Request node. This grades the memory summary itself, not the agent's reply — a summary that dropped the decision has found the regression even if the agent happened to answer correctly.

The observational-memory block retains the alert threshold as 4700 queued items. A summary that keeps the topic but loses the number is the specific failure this looks for, because the number is the thing the user cannot re-derive.

In its reply to the final turn, the agent names the HTTP Request node as the one chosen for posting the alert. Naming the native Slack node is the specific failure: it is the obvious answer, and the user ruled it out at the start of the conversation.
In its reply to the final turn, the agent gives the alert threshold as 4700 queued items. A different number — especially a rounder one like 5000 — means the figure did not survive.
The agent answers both parts from what it already has, rather than asking the user to repeat the decision or the threshold.
